newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea Daewoo Motor looks offshore to add capacity.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea Daewoo Motor looks offshore to add capacity.

text.p: With its annual domestic production capacity now at one million cars, the vehicle arm of South Korea's Daewoo Group has turned to emerging markets from Poland to China to expand production further.
"Our overseas projects are well in place. We are confident of making them successful," said Kim Tae-gou, chairman of Daewoo Motor.

The April opening of Daewoo's 300,000 vehicle plant in the southwestern city of Kunsan raised its total domestic capacity to one million vehicles, completing the automaker's scheduled investments at home.
Kim said Daewoo would jack up overseas production capacity to 1.5 million vehicles by 2000 from 600,000.
"Our investments have been welcomed by host countries because we are committed to their industrial development," Kim said.
Analysts applauded Daewoo's idea but warned of risk.

"Daewoo's globalisation is moving in the right direction given the domestic market's saturation, but it involves a lot of risk and fierce competition," said Kim Byoung-joon, an analyst at Dongwon Securities.

Since taking over Poland's state-owned vehicle maker Fabryka Samochodow Osobowych and Fabryka Samochodow Lublinie in 1995, Daewoo has raised their capacity to 200,000 a year. Daewoo's stake in the two firms stood at about 70 percent.
"The Polish venture is one of the most successful cases. Our products, much better now in quality, sell very well in the local market," Kim said.

Daewoo's vehicle production capacity in Poland is scheduled to triple by 2000. Daewoo officials said Daewoo's car sales in the country would top 200,000 vehicles this year, accounting for about 37 percent of the market, estimated at 530,000 units.
Another big playground for Daewoo is India where the Korean automaker's capacity was targeted to increase to 200,000 vehicles by 2000 from 70,000 units now.
"At the moment, purchasing power is still low. But India has great potential," Kim said.
Daewoo is expected to complete in late summer a parts plant capable of producing 300,000 engines and transmissions annually. Daewoo's share in the joint venture plant is 75 percent.
"Those parts would largely be exported to Vietnam, the Philippines and Uzbekistan," said Kim.
In China, Daewoo is slated to churn out engines and transmissions from 1999 at a rate of about 300,000 annually for sale locally and export to Southeast Asia.
"We also expect to produce finished cars in China some day," Kim said. He said China appeared to be impressed with Daewoo's rapid growth and performance in recent years.
In 1992, Daewoo Motor's total capacity was 200,000 vehicles, all produced in South Korea. "We now have so many visitors from China. They seem to trust us," Kim said.
Daewoo is currently producing cars in about 10 countries. Its future plans call for establishing production bases in Iran, Egypt and possibly the Ukraine, he said.
Kim said Daewoo's Romania's plant was now suffering from rising inventories because of a slump in the local market.
"Steep depreciation of Romania's currency eroded purchasing power in the country," he said.
Daewoo had planned to produce 70,000 cars in Romania, 40,000 for export and 30,000 for domestic sale, but Daewoo officials said local sales would fall far short of the target.
An engine and transmission plant in Romania is slated to begin production in December with an annual capacity of 300,000 each. They are to be exported to Poland, Uzbekistan and Russia.
